method: Each run: (1) cluster healthy (3 api Ready, 2 scheduler pods, no lease change for 30 s). (2) N open cases are inserted directly into the `closure` database as valid event logs in state patient_acknowledged (SLA book_confirmatory = 5 working days); their creation times are solved with the engine's own calendar so that a trigger falls due at a time drawn uniformly over the drill window, in three arms: A the state breach (mark_overdue + reminder rung), B the supervisor rung (breach and reminder already emitted earlier), C the coordinator rung (the first two rungs already emitted). So the sweep has new work to do continuously during the whole window. (3) A client issues, at a constant ~1 new case flow per second, create_case (client-chosen case_id), accept_ownership, contact_patient, patient_acknowledge (client-chosen event_id) and GET /cases/{id}, through the NodePort 127.0.0.1:18376 (kube-proxy spreads over the api pods); on a connection error, timeout or HTTP 5xx it retries the same request (same id) after 0.25 s, up to 90 s. (4) t0 = the instant the `kubectl delete pod <scheduler leader> <api-background leader>` command is issued (force: --grace-period=0 --force --wait=false, i.e. no graceful lease release; graceful: ordinary delete with the 30 s grace period, the processes release their leases on SIGTERM; hard: both containers are SIGKILLed through the node's runtime (crictl stop --timeout 0) and then the pods are force-deleted, t0 = the instant the SIGKILL commands were issued, so no process can release a lease; note that a plain --grace-period=0 delete still gives a container ~2 s between SIGTERM and SIGKILL, in which a process may release its lease: every run records lease_released_by_killed_holder). Leader identity comes from the leader_lease table (scheduler holder = pod name; the api-background holder is a random id mapped to its pod through the 'is now the leader' log line). (5) A poller reads leader_lease and the scheduler row of heartbeats every ~150 ms with the DATABASE clock (clock_timestamp()); t0 is converted to the database clock with the median host-minus-database offset of the run. time_to_new_leader_s = first poll at which the lease row names a holder other than the killed one with a higher fencing token, minus t0 (a takeover writes a fresh expiry, so that row is unexpired by construction); also reported: seconds since the killed holder's last renewal (its last observed expires_at minus the TTL). Resolution is the poll interval plus one query round trip. (6) Sweep evidence: the scheduler posts a heartbeat with sweeping=false at the end of every loop (after the sweep and the scans); the poller records every change of that row. sweep_gap_s = completion of the first sweep by a different holder than the killed leader minus completion of the killed leader's last sweep (the killed process can still finish a loop for a moment after t0: kubelet kill latency; sweep_gap_around_t0_s uses the last completion at or before t0 and the first after it instead, and killed_leader_last_sweep_after_t0_s says how long the killed leader kept sweeping). missed_sweeps = max(0, floor(sweep_gap_s / scheduler_interval_s) - 1): the number of whole scheduler intervals inside the gap in which a sweep should have started but did not, beyond the one interval that elapses between two healthy sweeps anyway. missed_sweeps_vs_baseline uses the median healthy gap of the run (interval + sweep + scans) instead of the nominal interval. The same gap is recomputed from the scheduler pods' log lines ('sweep sim_time=...') as a cross-check. (7) Late, not lost: after the window the expected scheduler events of every seeded case are computed by running the planner (app.sweep.plan_case) over the seeded log up to the verification time, until nothing more is planned; every expected event id must exist in the database (losses = expected and missing; unexpected = present and not expected), and re-planning every case from its STORED log must plan nothing (outstanding = 0). lateness = events.created_at (database insert time) minus the instant the trigger fell due. (8) Duplicates: duplicate event_id, duplicate (case, type, state-or-milestone, rung) scheduler events, duplicate (case, type) client events and duplicate genesis, over every seeded and client case; every acknowledged client request exists exactly once; every request that needed a retry produced exactly one event; every case replays (contiguous seq, replay_model succeeds, replay() state equals cases.current_state). (9) Fencing: every (holder, token) the poller saw for each lease; tokens must increase strictly; 409s are counted from the scheduler logs and the api access logs (organic = before the drill's own probes; 'sweep stopped: stale leader' log lines are sweeps the in-transaction fence stopped mid-way); a stale-token probe (killed holder, killed token) is sent to POST /scheduler/sweep and /scheduler/heartbeat after recovery and must get 409. The write-time fence (M7-1/F10: the store re-checks the lease with SELECT ... FOR SHARE inside the write transaction) is exercised directly: a due scheduler event is appended to a probe case through the real PostgresEventStore with three stale fences (killed holder+token, current holder + old token, killed holder + current token), each must raise StaleLeader and write zero rows, and a control append with the current fence must succeed. The event log does NOT record the holder or token of the scheduler that wrote an event, so 'no write from a deposed leader' is also shown by timing: every scheduler event's database created_at is placed inside the validity window of one observed lease token (acquired-at to last observed expiry) and the events outside every window are counted (strict, and with a tolerance of the longest observed loop, because the fence is checked when a sweep request ENTERS the API, not when it commits). (10) Client impact: attempts, error attempts (connection error, timeout, 5xx), retries, ops that never succeeded, maximum latency inside the disruption window [t0, time all 3 api pods are Ready again, polled with kubectl every ~0.5 s]. Pod log timestamps are taken to be in the same clock domain as the database (same Docker VM).

chart_values.lease_renewal_period: ttl/3 (scheduler lease keeper thread, api LeaderLoop)

Evidence: (1) the fence is checked when each scheduler request enters the API (require_current_leader) and again inside every write transaction (leader.check_fence_pg); the stale-token probe after recovery got HTTP 409 (sweep) and 409 (heartbeat), and the direct in-transaction probe: 3/3 stale fences refused with StaleLeader, 0 rows written by them, control write accepted=True; (2) every scheduler event's insert time lies inside a lease validity window (outside strict: 0, outside with 0.2s tolerance: 0); (3) event ids are deterministic, so a stale write could only be a no-op repeat.
